label: bm-buehler-materials-corpus
topic: What Buehler's materials papers say about design rules
summary: I clustered the 493 track-5 papers of the Buehler corpus (my keyword rules give 12 clusters; the largest are silk and filaments 118, collagen and bone 74, printed or machine-learning-designed hierarchical composites 70, and hierarchy, flaw-tolerance and size-effect work 69) and read abstracts or full texts for 15 of them, including 12 deep-dive papers: open-access full texts for the silk torsion, tendon, silica hierarchy, spider web, silk/HAP/chitin and plant-AI papers, and the two MIT PhD theses that contain the printed composite work. Result 1: the corpus is a source of design logic, not of resin or moisture numbers. None of 795 abstracts mentions vat-photopolymer, powder-bed or Formlabs printing (abstract-level; only 319 of 493 track-5 works have abstracts), 16 mention humidity-type stimuli, and no paper gives a hygroscopic expansion coefficient or diffusivity for a printed polymer. This confirms the earlier agents' gaps and does not fill them. Result 2: the printed composites traced to a printer (Dimas and Gu theses; Mirzaeifar 2015 says only multimaterial printing) came from Objet Connex single-print two-material jetting (VeroWhitePlus/VeroMagenta against TangoBlackPlus, moduli 2187 and 0.53 MPa, ratio 4126 by my arithmetic; nominal ratio about 1500 and effective 45-60 after interface mixing per Dimas), which Form 4 and Fuse 1+ cannot do. Result 3: four ideas transfer: stiffness ratio and soft/stiff topology as governing variables; a computational filter followed by a few printed tests (printed ML design about 25x tougher than the stiff material, 100,000 candidates screened); a formal reduction before printing with a test beyond the model (Brommer 2015); and humidity as a gated, hysteretic stimulus (silk threshold 68-70 % RH, five-cycle sweeps) with a coating that freezes a face (paraffin wax). Not transferable: molecular and nanometre rules (including the exponential defect-tolerance law, simulated at 27 x 70 micrometres), crystal misorientation, protein-sequence mechanisms, and the fabrication routes (jetting, PDMS ink writing at 160 C, nanofibril casting, mycelium growth). Deepening: with Buehler-style contrast (n = 1700-4100) the project's Timoshenko coefficient at equal thickness is only 0.4-0.9 % of the 3/2 ceiling and the optimum thickness ratio is 41-64, so the stiffness ratio that helps fracture hurts curvature. Cross-check of earlier agents: Flexible 80A V2 gains 8 % mass in 1 day in water by its own ASTM D471 data sheet, so "under 1 %" holds for the Formlabs solvent table (which lists only the older Flexible 80A at 0.7 %) but not for that resin; the 39.2 % IPA uptake of Elastic 50A V2 against under 0.1 % for Rigid 10K is confirmed on the re-fetched page.
lay_summary: Markus Buehler's group has written hundreds of papers on how bone, silk and shell get strong from their structure, and we searched them for rules that could guide a printed material that bends when the air turns damp. Almost none of the papers are about humidity, and none used the resin or powder printers that Formlabs sells; their printed samples came from a different machine that can spray a hard and a soft plastic in the same print. What carries over is the method: let a computer throw out bad designs, print only a few, test them, and write the rule you want to keep as a precise statement. One of our own calculations adds a warning: if the hard and soft plastics differ by a thousand times in stiffness, a two-layer strip of equal thickness curls about a hundred times less than the best possible, like a thermostat strip made of two metals that are far too unequal. So the demonstration should pick its two materials, and their thicknesses, together.

findings.claim: Spider dragline silk twists by more than 300 deg/mm when humidity rises past a threshold of about 70 % RH, independent of spider species (Liu et al. 2019, Buehler co-author). Natural protein fibre, not a printable resin.
findings.evidence_quote: We demonstrate that spider dragline silk exhibits a humidity-induced torsional deformation of more than 300°/mm. When the relative humidity reaches a threshold of about 70%, the dragline silk starts to generate a large twist

findings.claim: Measured thresholds for the three species: N. pilipes 68 %, A. versicolor and N. edulis around 70 %; the RH was cycled 40 -> 100 -> 40 % five times. Below threshold the fibre stays still, so the response is a gate, not a smooth ramp.
findings.evidence_quote: The threshold of RH for torsional actuation of the N. pilipes silk was 68%, as observed in the experiments

findings.claim: The twist is only partly reversible: when RH falls below threshold the N. pilipes silk keeps its twist, the other two species reverse it only slightly or noticeably. This is a hysteresis a bilayer law cannot represent.
findings.value: N. pilipes: twist maintained on drying
findings.evidence_quote: the twist deformation of the N. pilipes dragline silk was maintained, whereas the A. versicolor and N. edulis dragline silks reversed the twist slightly or rather noticeably

findings.claim: Tested fibres were micrometre-scale: N. pilipes 121 mm long and 3.1 +/- 0.1 um diameter; A. versicolor 87.9 mm long and 6.7 +/- 0.1 um. The result therefore says nothing about millimetre-thick printed sections, where diffusion time scales with thickness squared.
findings.evidence_quote: Torsional actuation of N. pilipes spider dragline silk (121 mm in length, 3.1 ± 0.1 μm in diameter)

findings.claim: Dragline silk is described as shrinking up to 50 % in length while its diameter roughly doubles at high humidity (supercontraction); the sign of axial strain is opposite to ordinary swelling.
findings.evidence_quote: dragline silk can shrink up to 50% in length concomitantly with radial swelling (about twofold increase of the diameter)

findings.claim: Molecular simulation attributes the twist to proline in the MaSp2 protein; this is a sequence-level mechanism with no direct analogue in an acrylate resin.
findings.evidence_quote: molecular simulations of MaSp1 and MaSp2 proteins in dragline silk reveal that the unique torsional property originates from the presence of proline in MaSp2

findings.claim: Giesa et al. 2017: dragline silk shrinks by up to 50 % along its axis in high humidity, and in-silico point mutations of polar or charged residues suppress or even reverse that supercontraction while keeping the mechanical properties. Simulation plus in situ mechanical and Raman tests; abstract only read.
findings.evidence_quote: they shrink along the main axis by up to 50% when exposed to high humidity, a phenomenon called supercontraction

findings.claim: Removing water from tendon collagen shortens the molecule and generates tensile stress from several MPa to almost 100 MPa, against about 0.3 MPa for contractile muscle (Masic et al. 2015, Buehler co-author). A measured upper bound on water-driven actuation stress in a natural polymer.
findings.evidence_quote: shortening of the molecule that translates into tensile stresses in the range of several to almost 100 MPa, largely surpassing those of about 0.3 MPa generated by contractile muscles

findings.claim: The paper converts relative humidity to osmotic pressure with the relation Pi = R T / v_m ln(RH) (v_m the molar volume of water), so the humidity stimulus can be expressed as a pressure on the polymer.
findings.evidence_quote: To allow the quantitative control of the osmotic pressure acting on the collagen fibre, we studied it in a chamber with controlled relative humidity (RH) that was then converted to osmotic pressure

findings.claim: Clamped tendon fibres built up 106 +/- 16 pN per molecule at 5 % RH. This is collagen, not a synthetic polymer.
findings.evidence_quote: Hindering the strain by clamping the fibre is, however, accompanied by a remarkable stress generation that reaches 106±16 pN per molecule at 5% RH

findings.claim: Ling et al. 2018: a designed-in-silico, self-assembled silk-nanofibril / hydroxyapatite / chitin-nanofibril nacre-like film reached 281 +/- 14 MPa strength and 22 +/- 2 MJ/m3 toughness at the 4:16 SNF/HAP:CNF ratio, 2-3x natural nacre strength.
findings.evidence_quote: the strength and toughness of 4:16 SNF/HAP:CNF nanocomposites reached 281±14 MPa and 22±2 MJ m −3

findings.claim: The same films were programmed into water-driven grab-and-release actuators because of their gradient structure and the water sensitivity of each component. This is the closest Buehler paper to a designed hygromorph bilayer; I could not read an actuation angle, curvature, RH or time from the main text, so no actuator number is reported.
findings.evidence_quote: these SNF/HAP:CNF nanocomposites can be programmed into "grab-and-release" actuators due to the gradient structure of the nanocomposites as well as the high water sensitivity of each of the components

findings.claim: Films were cast to about 10 um thickness at about 25 C and 50 % RH: a nanometre-fibril, water-cast process with no route onto a Form 4 or Fuse 1+.
findings.evidence_quote: allowed to dry at ~25°C and 50% relative humidity to give membranes of an approximate thickness of 10 μm

findings.claim: Sen and Buehler 2011 (atomistic-to-mesoscale simulation of silica): over up to four hierarchy levels the defect tolerance rises exponentially to about a hundred micrometres with no added material or mechanism; the base silica is brittle and sensitive to nanometre defects.
findings.evidence_quote: Over a range of up to four hierarchy levels, we find an exponential increase in the defect-tolerance approaching hundred micrometers without introducing additional mechanisms or materials.

findings.claim: The trade-off is stated: the biocalcite-like layout (soft nanoporous silica inclusions) gains defect tolerance at the cost of lower fracture strength than the bone-like layout. The soft phase here is a nanoporous form of the same silica, i.e. contrast made by porosity, not by a second chemistry.
findings.evidence_quote: the biocalcite-like structure shows a higher defect-tolerance at the cost of a lower fracture strength

findings.claim: Simulated geometry is micrometre scale (platelets 8.4 x 2.4 um by 100 nm; structure 27 x 70 um), and nothing was fabricated. The exponential law is a simulation result at a length scale 100-1000x below Form 4 or Fuse resolution.
findings.evidence_quote: The overall size of the structure considered here is 27 μm by 70 μm and 100 nm out-of-plane.

findings.claim: Dimas, Bratzel, Eylon, Buehler 2013: composites emulating bone, sponge and nacre topologies were printed in multi-material 3D printing at micrometre resolution from brittle base materials, and the soft/stiff topology alone raised fracture performance; model and test agree. Printed and tested.
findings.evidence_quote: The reported findings confirm that specific topological arrangements of soft and stiff phases as a design mechanism enhances the mechanical behavior in composites.

findings.claim: Dimas and Buehler 2014: the stiffness ratio of the two constituents is named as an important feature determining composite properties; DIC strain fields of printed composites were compared with simulation and plotted on Ashby diagrams.
findings.value: stiffness ratio is a governing variable
findings.evidence_quote: We elucidate the role of stiffness ratio variations of composite constituents as an important feature in determining the composite properties.

findings.claim: Thesis chapter of the same work (simulation): one composite designed at minimal cost has a toughness modulus eight times that of its constituents while keeping over 80 % of the Young modulus of the stiffest phase.
findings.evidence_quote: exhibits a fracture toughness modulus eight times larger than its constituents while retaining over 80% of the Young's modulus of its stiffest phase

findings.claim: Fabrication route: all specimens were printed on one Objet Connex500 multi-material printer in a single print from two acrylic photopolymers (VeroWhitePlus, TangoBlackPlus). A Form 4 or Fuse 1+ prints one material per job, so this fabrication route is not available on Formlabs hardware.
findings.evidence_quote: All specimens used in the study are printed at Objet Inc., in Billerica, MA, USA using an Objet Connex500TM multi-material 3D printer.

findings.claim: The nominal stiffness ratio of the two jetted materials is about 1500, but 3-4 % mixing at the interface lowers the effective ratio to 45-60; a ratio of 50 was used in the model. The interface is therefore a graded zone, not a sharp bimaterial joint.
findings.evidence_quote: Assuming an approximate 3-4% mixing of the two base materials at the interface an effective stiffness ratio between 45 and 60 is estimated, as apposed to ~1500.

findings.claim: Mirzaeifar, Dimas, Qin, Buehler 2015: more hierarchical levels in a stiff/soft composite, simulated and multimaterial-printed, retain a larger share of fracture strength with large edge cracks or many small defects, with a more uniform stress field. The abstract states no number.
findings.evidence_quote: We show that composites with more hierarchical levels dramatically improve the defect tolerance of the material.

findings.claim: Gu thesis Table 2.1 (adapted from a Buehler-group paper): VeroMagenta Young modulus 2187 +/- 404 MPa, strength 46.41 +/- 3.23 MPa; TangoBlackPlus 0.53 +/- 0.02 MPa, strength 0.72 +/- 0.04 MPa. The elongation row is column-scrambled in the PDF text and is not reported. Ratio of moduli by my arithmetic: 2187 / 0.53 = 4126.
findings.source: https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018) | local copy: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/buehler-papers/gu_thesis_mit_1721.1_119343.pdf
findings.evidence_quote: Young's rnodulus [MPa] 2187 404 0.53 0.02 Strength [MPa] 46.41 3.23 0.72 0.04

findings.claim: Printer for the Gu composites: Stratasys Objet500 Connex3 jetting two materials at once; printer resolution stated as about 10 micrometres in all directions.
findings.source: https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018) | local copy: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/buehler-papers/gu_thesis_mit_1721.1_119343.pdf
findings.evidence_quote: The resolution of the printer is on the order of 10 micrometers in all directions.

findings.claim: Gu, Takaffoli, Buehler 2017 (conch shell): a printed cross-lamellar prototype tested in a drop tower shows a second hierarchy level boosts impact performance by 70 % over a one-level hierarchy and 85 % over the stiff constituent; the mechanism is creation of crack-deviation paths.
findings.evidence_quote: adding the second level of cross-lamellar hierarchy can boost impact performance by 70% and 85% compared to a single-level hierarchy and the stiff constituent, respectively

findings.claim: In the thesis the same drop-tower study reports +85 % threshold impact energy for the two-level design versus the bulk stiff material, but only +10 % for the one-level design. My arithmetic 1.85 / 1.10 = 1.68, i.e. +68 %, matches the paper abstract's 70 %.
findings.source: https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018) | local copy: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/buehler-papers/gu_thesis_mit_1721.1_119343.pdf
findings.evidence_quote: the hierarchically superior Hier-2 design exhibits an 85% improve- ment with respect to the threshold impact energy in comparison with the bulk stiff material, while the threshold impact energy of the Hier-1 design is only 10% higher

findings.claim: Gu, Chen, Richmond, Buehler 2018 (Materials Horizons): a convolutional-neural-network design method for hierarchical composites, validated by additive manufacturing and testing. Abstract is a single sentence in Crossref.
findings.evidence_quote: A new approach to design hierarchical materials using convolutional neural networks is proposed and validated through additive manufacturing and testing.

findings.claim: Thesis chapter 7 (this work, "under review" in the thesis): the printed ML-chosen design was about 25x tougher than the stiff material, about 40x tougher than the soft material, and about 4x tougher than the best training design. Specimens are stiff/soft two-material 2D hierarchical grids.
findings.source: https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018) | local copy: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/buehler-papers/gu_thesis_mit_1721.1_119343.pdf
findings.value: ~25x vs stiff; ~40x vs soft; ~4x vs best training
findings.evidence_quote: the ML-designed hierarchical composite is approximately 25 times tougher than the stiff material and approximately 40 times tougher than the soft material.

findings.claim: The same chapter used a soft/stiff stiffness ratio of 0.01 and a stiff modulus of 1 GPa in simulation; the ML design space was 100,000 randomly generated hierarchical composites, each with an edge crack of 25 % of specimen width. The ML step is a filter: it ranks candidates, FEM and a printed test decide.
findings.source: https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018) | local copy: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/buehler-papers/gu_thesis_mit_1721.1_119343.pdf
findings.evidence_quote: A total of 100,000 hierarchical composites are randomly generated, which have an edge crack of 25% of the specimen width in the y-direction.

findings.claim: Chapter 6 surrogate accuracy: CNN above 98 % for toughness and strength, linear model 96 % and 95 %; but ranking, which matters for search, was not better with the CNN.
findings.source: https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018) | local copy: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/buehler-papers/gu_thesis_mit_1721.1_119343.pdf
findings.evidence_quote: The accuracies of the CNN model come out to be above 98% for both properties, which are at least 2% higher than the linear model with accuracies of 96% and 95% for toughness and strength, respectively.

findings.claim: Brute-force search is feasible only for tiny grids: for a 16-cell grid with 25 % soft (4 soft, 12 stiff) there are 1820 configurations (my check: C(16,4) = 1820).
findings.source: https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018) | local copy: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/data/buehler-papers/gu_thesis_mit_1721.1_119343.pdf
findings.evidence_quote: if the grid size is 16 and the volume fraction is 25 soft material (4 soft and 12 stiff elements) there are 1820 possible configurations

findings.claim: Qin, Compton, Lewis, Buehler 2015: the loading type dictates the optimal material distribution of a web; homogeneous threads are better for localized loading, stronger radial and weaker spiral threads for distributed loading; strength saturates at an asymptotic prey size. Simulation plus printed elastomer webs.
findings.evidence_quote: We show that the loading type dictates the optimal material distribution, that is, a homogeneous distribution is better for localized loading, while stronger radial threads with weaker spiral threads is better for distributed loading.

findings.claim: Peak force per mass peaks at 3.2 N/g when the spiral/radial thread diameter ratio is 1.26, and the study says d_s ~ d_r gives maximum web strength, consistent with measured garden-spider thread diameters of a few micrometres.
findings.evidence_quote: The peak value of 3.2 N g −1 is reached at d s / d r =1.26.

findings.claim: Webs were direct-ink-written in PDMS and cured at 160 C for 30 min; PDMS failure stress 6.8 MPa and failure strain 355 %. That is a syringe-extrusion elastomer process, not SLA resin or SLS powder.
findings.evidence_quote: Printed webs are cured at 160 °C for 30 min.

findings.claim: Brommer, Giesa, Spivak, Buehler 2015: category theory is used to keep a chosen molecular-mechanics relation (modulus scaling of 2D carbon allotropes) intact when moved to a macroscopic multi-material print, then validated by testing; the printed model was also twisted, a test outside the original model. This is the Buehler-group precedent for a formally stated reduction preceding a printed demonstrator.
findings.value: printed + tested; twist test beyond model
findings.evidence_quote: we use large-scale multi-material printing to examine the scaling of the elastic modulus of 2D carbon allotropes at the macroscale and validate our printed model using experimental testing

findings.claim: The paper states the logic of prototyping as a reduction: a prototype tests a subset of properties, and category theory maintains chosen information across scales or physical realizations. No proof assistant is involved; the check is by mechanical test.
findings.evidence_quote: as a prototype is not a complete product but rather a reduction to test a subset of properties

findings.claim: Luu et al. 2025 (arXiv 2508.06591): an LLM pipeline mined plant humidity-responsive systems (pollen paper, Rhapis excelsa leaves); LLM-generated procedures and predictions were tested in the lab, ending in a pollen-based adhesive with a measured shear strength.
findings.evidence_quote: culminating in the fabrication of a novel pollen-based adhesive with tunable morphology and measured shear strength

findings.claim: Only a qualitative adhesive result is given: pollen microgels between cardboard were shear-tested and the 2 % w/v sample was strongest; I found no numeric shear strength in the paper text.
findings.evidence_quote: the 2% w/v pollen concentration sample exhibited the highest adhesive shear strength.

findings.claim: A model prediction that paraffin wax would freeze the humidity response of pollen paper was confirmed in the lab: the wax-treated paper showed no significant observable response to humidity changes (qualitative; the humid test was 60 % to 20 % RH). Coating one face to disable swelling is a generic way to make a passive layer.
findings.value: paraffin wax coating blocks response; 60 -> 20 % RH
findings.evidence_quote: paraffin wax-treated pollen paper, as predicted, did not exhibit significant observable response to changes in humidity.

findings.claim: Lew et al. 2023: adjacent crystals in coral and nacre are misoriented by 1-40 deg; molecular dynamics of bicrystals puts the toughness maximum at 10, 20 and 30 deg for aragonite, vaterite and calcite. A crystallographic rule that needs self-assembling crystals, so it cannot be set by a printer.
findings.evidence_quote: aragonite, vaterite, and calcite exhibit toughness maxima when the bicrystals are misoriented by 10°, 20°, and 30°, respectively

findings.claim: Shen et al. 2024: an additively manufactured substrate colonised by mycelium gave a myco-composite with 160 MPa modulus and 0.72 MPa tensile strength, over 15-fold better than typical mycelium composites. A living-material route with a printed scaffold; it needs growth steps, not a resin.
findings.evidence_quote: our method yields the strongest mycelium composite reported to date with a modulus of 160 MPa and tensile strength of 0.72 MPa

findings.claim: Grezzana et al. 2020: simulation favours vertical osteon fibre layout under tension and twisted layout under compression; printed osteon-inspired samples suggest buckling-induced failure of vertically oriented fibres. A load-type-specific layout rule, shown qualitatively.
findings.value: vertical under tension; twisted under compression
findings.evidence_quote: Simulation results suggest a better performance of the vertical OM (VOM) under tensile loading and of the twisted OM (TOM) under compression

findings.claim: Printable pectin/chitosan/cellulose biotic composites degrade tunably: up to 100 % mass loss in 21 days in worm-laden soil, slower as chitosan content rises. The only hit in the track-5 abstracts that pairs 3D printing with a water or humidity environment, and it is about end-of-life, not actuation.
findings.value: up to 100 % mass loss in 21 d
findings.evidence_quote: demonstrated rapid degradation with up to 100% mass loss after 21 days for a pectin-based material buried in worm-laden oil

findings.claim: Bioinspired123D (arXiv 2603.29592): a language model writes Blender Python scripts for fabricable helical, cellular and tubular bioinspired geometries (dataset of over 4,000 scripts). It generates geometry, not material properties; useful for candidate shapes to feed a physics or Lean-checked filter.
findings.evidence_quote: We curate a domain-specific dataset of over 4,000 bioinspired and geometric design scripts spanning helical, cellular, and tubular motifs with parametric variability.

findings.claim: CONFIRMS spec-formlabs-materials.json and QUALIFIES spec-resin-chemistry.json: Flexible 80A Resin V2, ASTM D471 slab, 1 day in deionized water: hardness -26 Shore A, mass +8 %, volume +3 %; 1 week: -27, +9 %, +7 %. Read with pdftotext -table (the default layout scrambles the table).
findings.evidence_quote: Deionized Water 1 day -26 +8% +3% 94% 89%

findings.claim: The 0.7 % water figure belongs to the older Flexible 80A (V1) data sheet, a 1 cm cube weighed after 24 h. Formlabs' solvent table (parsed by the earlier agent) lists only "Flexible 80A Resin" with the same V1 numbers (acetone 37.4), not V2. So "every current SLA resin gains under 1 % in water" does not extend to Flexible 80A V2, whose own data sheet reports +8 % mass in 1 day by a different method (slab, wiped, no conditioning). Methods differ, so 0.7 vs 8 is not a clean 11x.
findings.evidence_quote: Diesel Fuel 2.3 Water 0.7

findings.claim: RE-CHECK of earlier claim (spec-resin-chemistry.json): the Formlabs solvent table lists Elastic 50A Resin V2 at 39.2 % isopropanol and Rigid 10K at under 0.1 %, and both Elastic 50A V2 and Flexible 80A Resin at 0.7 % water. Confirmed by parsing the page I re-fetched; the column order was read from the page header row (Water is the 18th solvent column, IPA the 10th).
findings.value: Elastic 50A V2: IPA 39.2 %, water 0.7 %; Rigid 10K: IPA <0.1 %

findings.claim: Rigid 10K row of the same page (the passive layer candidate): all solvent columns are 0.6 or below, including IPA and water.

OWN CALCULATION (calc.py): the Timoshenko coefficient f(m,n) is invariant under (m,n) -> (1/m,1/n) (max difference 2e-16 over a test grid) and a 400 x 301 log-grid search finds maximum f = 1.5000000000000002, so the 3/2 ceiling in the project record is reproduced numerically.

OWN CALCULATION: with the Buehler-style stiff/soft contrast an equal-thickness bilayer is nearly useless. f(1,n) = 0.0058 for n = 4126 (VeroMagenta/TangoBlackPlus, Gu thesis moduli), 0.0138 and 0.0126 for n = 1724 and 1897 (Rigid 10K / Flexible 80A V2 with the project's 5.8 MPa secant estimate), i.e. 0.4 % to 0.9 % of the 1.5 ceiling; at n = 50 (Dimas effective ratio) it is 0.375 (25 %), at n = 10 it is 0.996 (66 %, matching the earlier "34 % loss").

OWN CALCULATION: reaching the ceiling at such contrast needs m = n^(-1/2), a thickness ratio of 64 (n = 4126), 41.5-43.5 (n = 1724-1897), 7.1 (n = 50) or 3.2 (n = 10). With a 0.2 mm thin layer (Form 4 minimum wall in the project record) the thick layer would be 12.9, 8.3-8.7, 1.41 or 0.63 mm. The modulus ratio drops out of the curvature at the optimum, but it sets how thick the part must be. Timoshenko assumes small linear strain; the earlier agents note it over-predicts soft printed bilayers, so these are upper bounds.

OWN CALCULATION: osmotic pressure Pi = -(R T / v_m) ln(RH) at 25 C with v_m = 18.0 cm3/mol (water molar volume; unverified background constant): 166 MPa at 30 % RH, 95 MPa at 50 %, 49 MPa at 70 %, 14.5 MPa at 90 %, 7.1 MPa at 95 %, 1.4 MPa at 99 %, 0.41 MPa at 99.7 %. The thermodynamic driving pressure at room humidity is far above the roughly 0.3 to 100 MPa stresses Masic reports, so the limit on a printed layer is its sorption isotherm and stiffness, not the pressure.
findings.value: 49 MPa at 70 % RH; 0.4 MPa at 99.7 % RH

key_claims.claim: The Buehler corpus does not close the project's evidence gap: no abstract among the 795 fetched works mentions vat-photopolymer, powder-bed or Formlabs printing, only 16 mention humidity-type stimuli, and none reports a hygroscopic expansion coefficient or diffusivity for a printed polymer (abstract-level; 319 of 493 track-5 works have abstracts). Every printed-composite result I could trace to a printer (Dimas and Gu theses) used single-print multi-material jetting (Objet Connex), which Form 4 and Fuse 1+ do not offer; Mirzaeifar 2015 says only "advanced multimaterial 3D printing".
key_claims.source: own counts (corpus_stats.py) over buehler-corpus.json and buehler.json; https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/79497 (L. Dimas MIT thesis 2013)
key_claims.evidence_quote: All specimens used in the study are printed at Objet Inc., in Billerica, MA, USA using an Objet Connex500TM multi-material 3D printer.

key_claims.claim: What transfers is design logic: stiffness ratio and soft/stiff topology as governing variables, a computational filter followed by printed tests (printed ML-chosen design about 25x tougher than the stiff material), a formal reduction before printing (Brommer), and humidity as a gated, hysteretic stimulus tested by RH sweeps and cycles. Molecular, crystallographic and nanometre-scale rules do not transfer.
key_claims.evidence_quote: the ML-designed hierarchical composite is approximately 25 times tougher than the stiff material and approximately 40 times tougher than the soft material.

key_claims.claim: Buehler-style hard/soft contrast is incompatible with an equal-thickness hygromorph bilayer: with moduli 2187 and 0.53 MPa (ratio 4126) the Timoshenko coefficient at equal thickness is 0.0058, 0.4 % of the 3/2 ceiling, and the optimum thickness ratio is 64; for the Rigid 10K / Flexible 80A V2 pair (ratio about 1700-1900, project estimate) it is 41-44. This is my arithmetic on the project's Lean-checked formula, not a Buehler result.
key_claims.source: own calculation, script D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-buehler-materials-corpus/calc.py; moduli from https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119343 (G. X. Gu MIT thesis 2018)

key_claims.claim: Earlier-agent check: Flexible 80A Resin V2 is the exception to "stock Formlabs resins gain under 1 % in water in 24 h": its own data sheet (ASTM D471 slab) reports +8 % mass, +3 % volume and -26 Shore A after 1 day in deionized water, while the 0.7 % figure belongs to the older Flexible 80A in a different (cube) test. Data sheets re-fetched and sha256-matched this run.

recommendations: Treat the Buehler corpus as a source of design logic and test protocol, not of numbers: it contains no resin-moisture data, no hygroscopic expansion coefficient, no diffusivity, and (abstract-level) no vat or powder-bed printing. The coupon measurements the earlier agents asked for are still needed.

Use the corpus precedent to frame the proof of concept: Dimas, Gu and Brommer each close the loop model -> print -> test, and Brommer adds a test beyond the model. Our novelty is the machine-checked bound as the first filter, which no paper in this corpus has (abstract-level).

Choose the bilayer stiffness ratio on purpose. At n of about 1700-4100 (Buehler-style hard/soft jetting contrast) the optimum thickness ratio is 41-64 and an equal-thickness strip loses over 99 % of the curvature ceiling; prefer a soft/soft pair or measure wet moduli first, then fix m = n^(-1/2) within the 0.2 mm minimum wall.

Copy the Liu 2019 test protocol: sweep RH in steps, look for a threshold, cycle at least five times and record hysteresis; add a one-face wax or sealant coating coupon (Luu 2025) to confirm the passive layer.

Test the porosity-as-soft-phase idea (my inference from Sen & Buehler: soft nanoporous inclusions in the same silica) on a single material: SLS PA12 or SLA rigid coupons with lattice-density gradients, compared against the Timoshenko-type prediction. Not reported by any Buehler paper on Formlabs hardware.

Obtain the full text of Ling 2018 supplementary information and the Dimas 2014 / Gu 2018 papers through the library before any number from them is used in a claim; this report relied on abstracts plus the two MIT theses for those.

glossary.plain: A material or part that changes shape when the air gets more or less humid.
How full of water vapour the air is, as a percentage of the most it can hold at that temperature.
How many times stiffer one material is than another; 1000 means one is a thousand times harder to bend.
Two thin layers stuck together; if one swells more than the other the pair curls, like the metal strip in an old thermostat.
A proven upper limit on how tightly a two-layer strip can curl for a given swelling difference; the project checked it by computer.
Structure built in levels, like fibres twisted into threads twisted into rope.
How well a material keeps its strength when it has cracks or flaws.
How much energy a material soaks up before it breaks.
A printer that sprays two different plastics in the same print; the Formlabs printers named here use one material per print.
A fast statistical stand-in for a slow computer simulation, used to rank many designs.
A branch of mathematics about how structures map to one another while keeping chosen features.
The pull a material exerts on water; drier air means a stronger pull.
Two 3D-printing methods: light-cured liquid resin (SLA) and laser-fused powder (SLS).
Measuring how a surface stretches by comparing photos before and during a test.
Computer simulation that follows individual atoms.

Horiz., Brommer 2015, Lew 2023, Giesa 2017, Shen 2024, Grezzana 2020): only abstracts were read for the published versions. For Dimas and Gu the MIT PhD theses (hdl 1721.1/79497 and 1721.1/119343) were read in full text; thesis chapters may differ from the journal versions (the Gu thesis marks chapter 7 as under review).

Any numeric actuation value (curvature, angle, RH, time, cycles) for the grab-and-release actuator in Ling 2018: the main text I could read gives strength, toughness and modulus but the actuator result seems to sit in a figure or supplement that I did not read.
A numeric adhesive shear strength in Luu 2025: the paper text says only that 2 % w/v pollen was strongest.
The elongation row of Gu thesis Table 2.1: the PDF text interleaves the columns, so which elongation belongs to which material cannot be read; the moduli and strengths were read.

Any Buehler abstract with SLA, DLP, SLS, vat or Formlabs terms, and any hygroscopic expansion coefficient or water diffusivity for a printed polymer. The negative result is abstract-level only: 174 of the 493 track-5 works have no abstract in the corpus file, and I did not search full texts.

Whether the Objet/Connex photopolymers (VeroWhitePlus, TangoBlackPlus, VeroMagenta) absorb water: no Buehler paper reports it. So the Buehler printed-composite stiffness numbers cannot be transferred to humid conditions.

The JMPS 2026 category-theory paper was not re-read; its description (FFF bilayer strips, four angle comparisons) rests on the project record spec-marom-buehler-deep.json. I only confirmed via Crossref and the arXiv API that the DOI and arXiv entry exist.

A full read of the remaining roughly 120 track-5 papers that score 4 or 5: they were screened from the corpus "why" notes (and abstracts where present), not fetched, so the claim that the papers examined hold the most transferable ideas is a judgement, not an exhaustive test.
Independent confirmation of the Formlabs one-material-per-print limit: I rely on the project record (spec-formlabs-materials.json); I did not re-fetch a Formlabs statement on it.
